name: Gorila
tagline: Consolidates Brazilian brokerage accounts and investments into one portfolio view with returns, allocation and tax-season reporting.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The dashboard half of this is a weekend project: a trades table, a quote fetch, a time-weighted return calculation and some charts. The hard half is everything that makes the numbers correct in Brazil, specifically pulling positions out of brokers and B3, and then adjusting for splits, bonificações, subscriptions, amortizations, dividends and JCP across years of history. A local build that you feed manually will show you allocation and rough returns honestly and will probably satisfy anyone with twenty positions. It will not survive tax season, and it will quietly drift from reality the first time an issuer does something structurally weird. Build it if you want the view, not if you want the filing.
coreLoopDIY: A local app where you import or paste your trades, pulls daily quotes from a public Brazilian market API, and shows consolidated position, allocation and return over time.
requirements: A quote source for B3 tickers and funds, for example a public market data API with a free tier
Manual entry or CSV import of your own trade history, including the old stuff
Patience for corporate actions, which you will be adjusting by hand
Fixed income and offshore assets modeled as whatever you decide they are
whatYouLose: Automatic broker and B3 position sync, so every new trade is your problem
Corporate action handling that is already right, splits and bonuses and spinoffs included
Tax-season outputs sized for Brazilian reporting, which is the reason most people subscribe
Coverage of exotic assets: funds, debentures, COE, crypto, foreign holdings, pension plans
Someone else maintaining asset master data when tickers change or funds merge
moatNotes: The asset registry and corporate action history is the actual product. Everything visual sits on top of it.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the chart is not the value, the reconciliation is. Getting a decade of trades across three brokers to agree with what B3 thinks you own, with every split and dividend applied in the right order, is grinding data work that nobody wants to redo every April. Paying someone to keep that registry current, and to emit numbers you can transcribe into a tax filing without sweating, is cheaper than the weekend you would spend discovering that your homemade average cost is wrong.
notes: Great weekend build for the view, bad weekend build for the filing.
prompt:
Build a local-first personal investment portfolio tracker for Brazilian market assets. Single developer, runs on my laptop, no accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Python 3.12, FastAPI, Jinja2 templates, HTMX for interactions, SQLite via SQLModel.
- Chart.js from a CDN for charts. No React, no build step.
- uv for dependency management, a single `uv run` command to start on localhost:8000.

Data model:
- assets: ticker, name, class (stock, FII, ETF, fixed_income, cash, other), currency.
- transactions: date, asset, side (buy, sell), quantity, unit_price, fees, note.
- events: date, asset, type (dividend, jcp, split, reverse_split, bonus, amortization), factor or cash_per_share.
- quotes: asset, date, close.

Features that are in scope:
- CSV import of transactions with a documented column layout, plus a manual add form.
- Manual entry form for corporate action events, applied chronologically when computing positions.
- Average cost per position using Brazilian weighted average cost, adjusted by splits and bonuses.
- Daily quote refresh from brapi.dev using a token read from .env (BRAPI_TOKEN). Cache quotes in SQLite, never refetch a date you already have.
- Dashboard: total market value, total invested, unrealized result, allocation pie by class and by asset, portfolio value line chart over time.
- Per asset page: position history, transactions, events, realized and unrealized result.
- Income report: dividends and JCP received per month and per year, table plus CSV export.

Out of scope, do not attempt:
- Broker or B3 scraping, any login automation, any credential storage.
- Tax forms, DARF calculation or IR filing output. Print a disclaimer saying numbers are informational.
- Multi user, auth, hosting.

Also produce: schema migrations on startup, a seed script with 10 fake transactions and 2 corporate actions, pytest tests for average cost and split adjustment math, and a README that states plainly what the tracker gets wrong.
